Penton (Sclerophrys pentoni) is a small to medium-sized bufonid found across the Sahelian savannahs of West Africa. Field surveys indicate that females attain a maximum snout-urostyle length of 7.65 centimeters [Li = 7.65 centimeters], although the species exhibits considerable variation in adult body size, with the typical range for females extending from 5.8 to 9.5 centimeters. Males are notably more diminutive, reaching an ultimate total length of 7.0 centimeters [Li = 7.0 centimeters], with documented values varying between 5.4 and 7.4 centimeters across its geographic range. Newly metamorphosed toadlets emerge from the aquatic environment at a minute wet weight of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a consequence of the relatively small egg diameter of roughly two millimeters. This negligible birth mass underscores the substantial energetic and size-based developmental trajectory the species must complete before reaching adulthood.

At a stable thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring just five days [ab = five days] after egg deposition. This brief incubation period is consistent with the fast developmental rates observed in other tropical bufonids under warm, stable temperatures. Following an aquatic tadpole phase characterized by herbivorous grazing on periphyton and detritus, the larval-juvenile transition is completed through metamorphic climax. The age at which individuals attain sexual maturity following this transformation has been estimated at two years after metamorphosis [tp = two years after metamorphosis] when maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a value that reflects the moderate pace of maturation typical of arid-zone amphibians that must balance rapid development against seasonal constraints on foraging and growth.

Adult body mass in this species demonstrates a pronounced sexual dimorphism, consistent with the pattern observed in snout-urostyle length. The ultimate wet weight attained by females reaches 34.83 grams [Wwi = 34.83 grams], a mass derived from allometric scaling relationships among congeneric bufonids. Males, being structurally smaller, achieve a maximum adult wet mass of 26.7 grams [Wwi = 26.7 grams], which represents roughly three-quarters of the female asymptotic weight. This disparity in mass is likely linked to the energetic demands of gamete production in females, who must allocate considerable resources toward egg development. The body condition of adults fluctuates seasonally, with peak masses recorded immediately following the summer rains when invertebrate prey becomes abundant across the ephemeral pools and grasslands they inhabit.

Reproductive output has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Gravid females produce a single clutch of 330 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = 330 eggs per reproductive event], and in the laboratory they are capable of depositing approximately 0.9 clutches per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.9 clutches per day]. The maximum longevity recorded for this species under these same laboratory conditions is approximately six years [am = approximately six years] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a lifespan that falls within the range documented for other medium-sized bufonids in captivity. This extended reproductive window, combined with the substantial per-clutch investment, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes periodic high fecundity, likely an adaptation to the unpredictable rainfall patterns that characterize its Sahelian habitat.

Seasonal reproductive activity in Penton is tightly coupled to the onset of the wet season, when temporary water bodies become available for egg deposition and larval development. The timing of first reproduction after metamorphosis has been estimated at roughly two years [tR = roughly two years], a duration that aligns with the species' attainment of sexual maturity. While the laboratory data provide a controlled baseline for understanding these life-history parameters, field observations suggest that natural thermal regimes and variable food availability may modulate both growth rates and reproductive schedules. Future comparative studies between Sahelian and more mesic populations of bufonids would help clarify the extent to which these life-history traits represent plastic responses to environmental aridity versus fixed adaptations within the clade.
